Dwarf of the frontier. Takes and deals the most harm and wears any armour. Brawn: lifts what has fallen and wrenches what is stuck.

WHY YOU HAVE COME

Coming home
Your father, a drover of Muzgavor, went out on the road with the cart and did not come home. You have come back to Muzgavor for the first time in three years.
The brothers' errand
The brothers of your order have sent you to Ramkom with a letter for the priest, and an errand: to copy the old writing at Luncustod, which no one has ever copied.
What is owed
You owe Fargrim, at Ramkom, thirty coin for a cart of peat that you lost on the road last spring. You have come back to pay it, somehow.
Over the hills
You have come over the hills into Coldmoor with your trade and not much else, to see what there is for someone who will work.

Coming home makes you a herdsman, who knows woodcraft.

The bailey of Ramkom is a muddy yard inside a wall, with the hall on one side and the stables on the other, and everybody in it is either on duty or pretending to be. It stands looking out over the Dagzârameth, with the fells at its back.

The market-place of Brethelmasto

Brethelmasto has a market cross in the middle of a square trodden bare, and round the square houses with their ground floors given over to shops and their upper floors to people shouting down from them. It grew up where the Saersîr runs into the Nûrrant.

A plank door, barred on the outside.

Brethelmasto is where the roads of the country meet, and so where its goods do: whatever is made in the country is bought and sold here at least once. Two merchants are shaking hands on a bargain, and each is looking over the other’s shoulder for a better one.

The ford at Tatharimlad

You set out from the ford of the Nûrrant.

Partway, the road goes down to the water and through it, and up the far bank with your boots full.

Tatharimlad is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are.

The road runs down between the houses of Tatharimlad to the Landsîr, goes straight in, and comes out on the far bank darker and wetter. Every house on this side has something to sell to people who have just come out of a river. It grew up where the Landsîr runs into the Nûrrant. By the track stands the wayside shrine of Boann: a humble fountain, small and weathered, with offerings of honey before it.

A shepherd’s boy is telling anyone who will listen that something comes up out of Silkholme sink at night and takes a ewe off a cave in the hillside in Eregtaur, and that Garth means to burn it out.

Two philosophers are disputing here, and a crowd stands round them: Dayereth, who holds that all things are one and change is only seeming, and Lia, who holds that nothing stays. Quarion leans between them with folded arms, and laughs at both.

The bell is gone from its frame over the well. ‘Hobs,’ people say, and spit, and nobody has gone after it.

The Nûrrant runs knee-deep and clear over the ford stones. The Nûrrant runs knee-deep and clear over the ford stones. Tatharimlad is here because the road has to cross the Landsîr somewhere, and here it can. The crossing came first, and the houses came after to sell the crossing what it wanted. A carter stands in the water with his breeches rolled, coaxing a horse that has decided against it.

‘Tatharimlad,’ says Epona, and stands a moment where the track comes in. ‘Smaller than it was.’

Veyas looks up from the offerings and goes still, then laughs. ‘Epona. The god has a sense of humour.’ There is a blessing for the company, and bread from the offerings for the road.

Smut winds once round your ankles and goes off about her business.

FLOWERHOLT
EVENING · COLD
2 WOLFMOON

Rosaturris

It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost.

The path climbs onto open moor, and the country falls away behind you in long brown folds.

A lone tower stands above the land. Wild goats stand on rock no goat should stand on. Over the door, cut in the old script: ROSATURRIS.

The keep is bare stone, cracked by frost. A light burns at the top of its tower. To one side of the gate the curtain wall has slumped into a breach of loose stone. Behind the keep, a well-head is half buried in nettles. Low in the tower’s footing is a postern, barred from within, with an old lock on it. A rusted portcullis hangs across the gate passage, a foot short of the ground.

Rosaturris: a lone tower in Sigakwinde. The name is Aenean, the old tongue, for “rose tower”.

‘Somebody should make a song about that place,’ says Epona. ‘Somebody probably did, and it was sad.’

The shadows are long when you leave the foot of Sigakwinde by Tatharimlad, and getting longer.

Night comes on while you are still on the path. An owl keeps pace with you for a while, and then thinks better of it.

Tatharimlad is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are.

Dayereth no longer teaches the One: things end, Dayereth tells whoever will listen, and the end of them is not seeming.

label: journey1-mine
body:
FLOWERHOLT
MORNING · COLD
3 WOLFMOON

Argentumons

It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost.

The path follows the river a while, close enough to hear it, and crosses where it runs wide and shallow.

Spoil heaps run down the hillside in grey fans that the heather has never taken, and above them a timbered mouth opens into the hill, its lintel a single oak beam. Cut into the beam in the old script, worn but whole: ARGENTUMMONS.

This is Argentumons, as the folk call it.

The heather stops a long stride short of the adit mouth all round, as though it had been burned back, and grows again beyond. Nothing nests in the spoil.

Immeral sees it first. There is no track into the adit that is not a man’s, and the foxes’ runs bend wide of it. Only at noon, with the sun full on the hillside, do the ravens come down and sit on the spoil.

Reeds hiss in the wind. The frogs stop, all at once, and start again behind you.

Rolen looks at it the way a soldier looks at a wall: where it would break, and who would be standing there when it did.

Spoil heaps run down the hillside in grey fans that the heather has never taken, and above them a timbered mouth opens into the hill, its lintel a single oak beam. Cut into the beam in the old script, worn but whole: ARGENTUMMONS.

This is Argentumons, as the folk call it.

The heather stops a long stride short of the adit mouth all round, as though it had been burned back, and grows again beyond. Nothing nests in the spoil.

Immeral sees it first. There is no track into the adit that is not a man’s, and the foxes’ runs bend wide of it. Only at noon, with the sun full on the hillside, do the ravens come down and sit on the spoil.

Carmencaw

You set out from the edge of Deopwudu by Guldhricg early, with your shadow long in front of you on the path.

Partway, the path goes down to the water and through it, and up the far bank with your boots full.

A cave opens in the hillside, its mouth as round as a sung O and as smooth as the inside of a shell, without a mark of chisel anywhere. Over it, cut in the old script: CARMENCAVUS.

This is Carmencaw, as the folk call it.

When the wind gets up the hill gives out a note, low and long, that sets the dogs howling in the valley. The sheep will not graze its slope.

Nothing nests within earshot of the hill’s note. The rooks go round it, and the deer will not drink from the stream below it.

An owl watches from a hollow oak, and does not blink.

‘If there is writing in there,’ says Jade, ‘I want to see it before anybody else breathes on it.’

The ford at Guldhricg

You set out from the edge of Deopwudu by Guldhricg early, with your shadow long in front of you on the path.

Guldhricg is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are.

At Guldhricg the road and the Albestrēam meet, and the houses stand close along the bank to watch them do it. A rope is strung across the water on posts for anyone who misjudges the depth. It grew up where the Albestrēam runs into the Chealdbrōc, with the fells at its back. By the track stands the wayside shrine of Coventina: a cracked altar, small and weathered, with offerings of tin before it. The Albestrēam runs knee-deep and clear over the ford stones. Guldhricg is here because the road has to cross the Albestrēam somewhere, and here it can. The crossing came first, and the houses came after to sell the crossing what it wanted. Someone on the far bank is shouting a question across the water. Nobody on this side can make out what it is, and several people are answering it anyway.

Jade looks round Guldhricg as if counting it, and seems satisfied that it is all still there.

‘Jade! Look at you.’ Ghokarn shuts the shop for the length of a cup, asks after everything at once, and will not let you leave without food for the road.

Shadow barks twice, for form’s sake, then comes to see who you are.
